description: Events from P. M. Rattansi (Ambix 1966) on alchemy in Raleigh's History of the World, and Lynn Thorndike (Ambix 1938) on alchemy in the first half of the sixteenth century. Covers Pantheus's Ars Transmutationis (1518), Pantheus's Voarchadumia (1530), and Raleigh's chemical laboratory in the Tower of London (1605-1616).

persons.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
persons.bio_html:
Sir Walter Raleigh (c. 1552–1618) was an English courtier, soldier, colonial adventurer, historian, and natural philosopher whose chemical investigations, particularly during his imprisonment in the Tower of London (1603–1616), made him one of the most famous lay practitioners of alchemy and iatrochemistry in early modern England. P. M. Rattansi, in his study of alchemy and natural magic in Raleigh's History of the World (Ambix, 1966), reconstructs Raleigh's chemical activities from contemporary sources: Sir William Wade, lieutenant of the Tower, reported to Robert Cecil in 1605 that Raleigh had converted 'a little hen-house in the garden into a still-house; and here he doth spend his time all day in distillations.' The Diary of the Rev. John Ward (1661) records that Ward met a Mr. Sampson who had served as 'operator to Sir Walter Raleigh twelve years, whilst he was in the Tower' — an account that attests both the sustained duration of Raleigh's chemical work and the institutional character of his laboratory with its dedicated assistants.

Raleigh's most lasting chemical legacy was 'Raleigh's Cordial,' a complex pharmaceutical preparation whose recipe circulated throughout the seventeenth century. John Evelyn recorded in 1662 accompanying King Charles II to the laboratory of the royal chemist Nicolas Le Febvre to witness 'his accurate preparation of Sir Walter Raleigh's Cordial'; Le Febvre published a Discours sur le Grand Cordial de Sr. Walter Rawleigh in 1665, describing its preparation and virtues. Raleigh's chemical interests were not incidental to his broader intellectual life: his enormous History of the World (1614), composed during his imprisonment, explicitly connected chemical methods of analysis — 'as a skilful and learned Chymist can as well by separation of visible elements draw helpful medicines out of poison, as poison out of the most helpful herbs and plants' — to his historical method of separating truth from legendary accretion. Rattansi analyzes the History as a document of Raleigh's engagement with Hermeticism, neo-Platonic natural magic, and the alchemical tradition, demonstrating that his imprisonment transformed Raleigh into one of the most intellectually ambitious natural philosophers of the Jacobean period.

Raleigh was released from the Tower in 1616 for an expedition to South America in search of the legendary gold of El Dorado; when the expedition failed and an attack on Spanish settlements violated treaty terms, he was executed in 1618 under his original sentence from 1603. His chemical work in the Tower thus represents the most sustained phase of his natural-philosophical activity, conducted under conditions of enforced leisure that gave him time for systematic experimentation and historical writing.

texts.title: Voarchadumia contra Alchimiam
texts.analysis_html:
Voarchadumia contra Alchimiam: Ars distincta ab Archimia et Sophia (Venice, 1530) by the Venetian priest and gold-refiner John Augustine Pantheus (Giovanni Agostino Panteo) is a remarkable document of sixteenth-century efforts to practise and publish alchemy while navigating ecclesiastical and civil prohibitions. Lynn Thorndike, in his survey of alchemy in the first half of the sixteenth century in Ambix (1938), identifies the Voarchadumia as Pantheus's response to the authorities' objections to his earlier Ars Transmutationis Metallicae (Venice, 1518): following the public circulation of his 1518 work, attention was drawn to the existence of a papal decretal and a Venetian decree against alchemists — specifically the Extravagans of Pope John XXII opening 'Spondent quas non exhibent divitias pauperes alchimistae,' the constitution of Emperor Constantine against counterfeiters, and the decree of the Council of Ten against alchemists. Pantheus's solution was to publish a new work in 1530 that claimed to deal not with alchemy at all, but with 'Voarchadumia' — an art he represented as the true wisdom hidden behind alchemy's impostures, 'a kind of cabala of metals' handed down from Tubal Cain through the Chaldeans and Indians. The Voarchadumia was said to be 'an art distinct from alchemy,' its title ostentatiously proclaiming itself to be contra alchimiam — against alchemy.

Thorndike notes the striking paradox: despite this aggressive disclaimer, the Voarchadumia repeats most of the material of Pantheus's 1518 work, now reframed in a Kabbalistic vocabulary that allowed the same alchemical procedures to be presented as belonging to a different and supposedly legitimate art. The volume includes woodcuts of alchemical furnaces and apparatus and a bird's-eye view of Venice and its surroundings; Pantheus again obtained permission to print from the Apostolic Legate and the Council of Ten. Both the Voarchadumia and the 1518 work were reprinted together at Paris in 1550 and again in the second volume of Zetzner's Theatrum Chemicum as published in 1613 and 1659. The Voarchadumia thus represents a documented strategy of terminological and classificatory camouflage that allowed the continued practice and publication of alchemical knowledge within a regulatory environment hostile to the art under its traditional name.

events.title: Pantheus Publishes Ars Transmutationis Metallicae at Venice
events.description: John Augustine Pantheus (Giovanni Agostino Panteo), a Venetian priest and licensed gold-refiner, published his Ars Transmutationis Metallicae at Venice in December 1518, with the authorization of Pope Leo X and the permission of the Council of Ten. Lynn Thorndike, in Ambix (1938), records the title page as bearing 'Ars transmutationis metallicae cum Leonis X ponti. max. et conci. capi. decemvirorum Venetorum edicto,' and notes that the work culminated in a secondary 'Commentary of the Theory of the Metallic Art of Transmutation' addressed to a noble Pole named William Hyerosky. Pantheus cites a diverse range of alchemical authorities including the Turba Philosophorum, Geber, Alphidius, Avicenna, Rhodianus, and others, some available to him only in manuscript. Thorndike identifies the work as an unusually ambitious attempt to publish alchemical theory in print under explicit papal and civic patronage, obtained at a moment when Pope Leo X's broad Medici patronage of arts and learning extended to alchemy. Pantheus describes himself as 'a priest but a refiner of gold of Venice,' combining ecclesiastical and artisanal identities. Within about a decade, however, objections were raised at the papal or Venetian court about the existence of anti-alchemical prohibitions, leading Pantheus in 1530 to publish a rebranded version of much the same material under the title Voarchadumia, which he claimed was an art entirely distinct from alchemy.
events.scholarly_grounding: Lynn Thorndike analyzed the Ars Transmutationis Metallicae and its context in 'Alchemy During the First Half of the Sixteenth Century' in Ambix vol. 2 no. 1 (1938) pp.26-38.

events.title: Pantheus Publishes Voarchadumia to Circumvent Anti-Alchemy Laws
events.description: In 1530 John Augustine Pantheus published Voarchadumia contra Alchimiam: Ars distincta ab Archimia et Sophia at Venice — a rebranded version of his 1518 alchemical work that claimed to present not alchemy but 'Voarchadumia,' a distinct art he defined as a 'cabala of metals' handed down from Tubal Cain through the Chaldeans. Lynn Thorndike, in Ambix (1938), identifies this as a direct response to challenges raised at the papal or Venetian court about his 1518 publication in light of existing prohibitions: specifically, the Extravagans of Pope John XXII opening 'Spondent quas non exhibent divitias pauperes alchimistae,' the Emperor Constantine's constitution against counterfeiters, and the Venetian Council of Ten's decree against alchemists. Despite the Voarchadumia's title explicitly announcing itself as against alchemy (contra alchimiam), Thorndike notes that Pantheus 'repeats most of his work of 1518 in the course of the Voarchadumia,' with the same procedures now reframed in Kabbalistic vocabulary. The work includes woodcuts of alchemical furnaces and apparatus, a bird's-eye view of Venice, and again obtained permission to print from the Apostolic Legate and the Council of Ten. Both works were reprinted together at Paris in 1550 and in Zetzner's Theatrum Chemicum (1613, 1659), attesting to their lasting authority in the printed alchemical canon. The episode is a documented case of the regulatory pressures that shaped alchemical publication in the early sixteenth century and the strategies practitioners devised to navigate them.
events.scholarly_grounding: Lynn Thorndike analyzed the Voarchadumia and its context in 'Alchemy During the First Half of the Sixteenth Century' in Ambix vol. 2 no. 1 (1938) pp.26-38.

events.title: Walter Raleigh's Chemical Laboratory in the Tower of London
events.description: During his imprisonment in the Tower of London (1603–1616), Sir Walter Raleigh (c. 1552–1618) maintained a systematic chemical laboratory, making him one of the most thoroughly documented lay alchemical-chemical practitioners in Jacobean England. P. M. Rattansi, in Ambix (1966), reconstructs the laboratory's activities from contemporary sources: Sir William Wade, lieutenant of the Tower, reported to Robert Cecil in 1605 that Raleigh had converted 'a little hen-house in the garden into a still-house; and here he doth spend his time all day in distillations.' The Reverend John Ward's Diary (1661) records his meeting with Mr. Sampson, who 'was operator to Sir Walter Raleigh twelve years, whilst he was in the Tower' — establishing that the laboratory operated with a dedicated professional assistant for over a decade and constituted a genuine research enterprise rather than casual experimentation. Raleigh's laboratory produced the preparation known as 'Raleigh's Cordial,' which became famous throughout the seventeenth century: John Evelyn recorded in 1662 accompanying King Charles II to witness Nicolas Le Febvre's preparation of the Cordial, and Le Febvre published a formal treatise on its preparation and virtues in 1665. Raleigh himself connected his chemical method to his historical method in the History of the World (1614), comparing a 'skilful and learned Chymist' who 'by separation of visible elements' draws medicine from poison to the historian who extracts truth from legend. Rattansi situates Raleigh's chemical activity within his broader engagement with Hermeticism, Paracelsian natural philosophy, and the tradition of natural magic, identifying the History of the World as a key document of early seventeenth-century English attitudes toward alchemy and its relationship to legitimate natural knowledge.
events.scholarly_grounding: P. M. Rattansi analyzed Raleigh's chemical activities in the Tower from primary sources in 'Alchemy and Natural Magic in Raleigh's History of the World' in Ambix vol. 13 no. 3 (1966) pp.122-138.

events.title: Publication of Raleigh's History of the World
events.description: Sir Walter Raleigh's History of the World, composed during his imprisonment in the Tower of London and published in April 1614, contained a systematic engagement with alchemy, Hermeticism, and neo-Platonic natural magic that P. M. Rattansi, in Ambix (1966), analyzes as a major document of early seventeenth-century English attitudes toward the occult sciences. Rattansi demonstrates that the History presents Raleigh's engagement with the Florentine Platonic tradition — particularly Ficino's neo-Platonism with its postulate of a universe 'shot through with secret sympathies and antipathies' — as the natural-philosophical framework within which chemical investigations made sense. Raleigh defends the secrecy with which alchemists guarded their knowledge, refers to the 'secret virtues hidden in nature which the chemists sought to put to human use,' and explicitly uses the figure of the chemist as an analogy for the historian's method: as a skilled chemist draws medicine from poison by 'separation of visible elements,' so the historian extracts truth from legend. James I suppressed the first edition of the History — commanding it to be called in 'for divers exceptions, but specially for beeing too sawcie in censuring princes' — but the book continued to circulate and was reissued in a second edition (1628) and subsequent printings throughout the seventeenth century. Rattansi situates the History in relation to James I's very different views on natural magic and demonology (expressed in his Daemonologie, 1597) and to Francis Bacon's contemporaneous programme for the reform of natural philosophy, arguing that Raleigh's Hermetic-Paracelsian framework represents an intellectual position distinct from both Jacobean demonology and Baconian empiricism.
events.scholarly_grounding: P. M. Rattansi analyzed the History of the World's engagement with alchemy and natural magic in 'Alchemy and Natural Magic in Raleigh's History of the World' in Ambix vol. 13 no. 3 (1966) pp.122-138.
